<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential in multi-agent negotiation tasks, yet evaluation in this domain remains challenging due to a lack of robust and generalizable benchmarks. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce a negotiation benchmark based on Scoreable Games, with the aim of developing a highly complex and realistic evaluation framework for LLMs. Our work investigates the reproducibility of claims in their benchmark, and provides a deeper understanding of its usability and generalizability. We replicate the original experiments on additional models, and introduce additional metrics to verify negotiation quality and evenness of evaluation. Our findings reveal that while the benchmark is indeed complex, model comparison is ambiguous, raising questions about its objectivity. Furthermore, we identify limitations in the experimental setup, particularly in information leakage detection and thoroughness of the ablation study. By examining and analyzing the behavior of a wider range of models on an extended version of the benchmark, we reveal insights that provide additional context to potential users. Our results highlight the importance of context in model-comparative evaluations.</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Equal contribution.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The growing use of LLMs in multiagent systems has spurred demand for robust evaluation benchmarks. While existing benchmarks assess capabilities such as reasoning and task completion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">White et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, their ability to measure nuanced social interactions, such as negotiation and consensus-building, remains understudied. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brookins and DeBacker (2023)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Akata et al. (2023)</a></cite> investigate LLM behavior in structured negotiation games, however they primarily make use of simple prisoner’s dilemma scenarios that necessitate greater effort to generalize to complex real world negotiations. As these benchmarks are also static, their relevance is also called into question as increasingly powerful LLMs are released. For this reason, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davidson et al. (2024)</a></cite> employs a dynamic benchmark with adjustable complexity. However, their scope is limited to the case of only two negotiating agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In response, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduce a benchmark<span id="footnotex3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
          Original implementation: https://github.com/S-Abdelnabi/LLM-Deliberation</span></span></span> grounded in Scoreable Games <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Susskind, 1985</a>)</cite>, a round-based multi-agent discussion format designed to teach negotiation. This proposed framework evaluates the ability of LLMs to reach agreements through role-based dialogue, which offers a promising tool for assessing cooperation in real world multi-agent settings.
However, the usability of such benchmarks hinges on how well the experiments generalize, and how fair the outcomes are to each model. More specifically, usability depends on how wide the range of models the benchmark is capable of evaluating, and whether a user can derive consistent comparisons between models using the benchmark.
There are a multitude of articles that highlight the gaps in LLM benchmarking in general, including the risk of leakage <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and inconsistent metric rigor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which can invalidate benchmark results and create unfair comparison models. However, few studies critically evaluate negotiation-focused benchmarks such as the one proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we reproduce and extend the work of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite><span id="footnotex4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
            
            
            
          Our implementation: https://github.com/joshrosie/FACT29</span></span></span>. Our contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A reproduction study analyzing the ability of the benchmark to generalize across a wider variety of untested models, exposing and addressing gaps in weaker model evaluation and replicating adversarial LLM behaviors;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Identification of unfair comparisons in the original experimental setup due to inconsistent model performance across benchmark dimensions and sensitivity to ablation configurations;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finding and fixing several technical limitations in the code;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Enhanced evaluation transparency via supplementary scoring metrics;</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Demonstration of the limited adaptability of the framework through a lack of game diversity.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Scope of reproducibility</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmark proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> aims to study the capabilities of LLMs to cooperate and negotiate through a round table format of competition, where agents are instructed to keep their preferences hidden. Moreover, through altering prompts, score functions, and behavioral characteristics, the authors claim the benchmark can be easily adaptable to suit the testing requirements of new models. As an open source benchmark, the original work provides further transparency on the capabilities of language models to negotiate through empirical evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Drawing on frameworks for benchmark evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reuel et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we operationalize concerns of generalizability and fairness into testable claims and validate them through experiments across several models and negotiation scenarios.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Claims</h3>

<div id="S2.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We aim to address a series of claims, both implicit and explicit, that we identify in the original paper. The claims are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using the framework provided, a user can objectively compare skills in multi-agent negotiation between different LLMs. This claim will be referred to as the <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">benchmark claim</span>. We demonstrate that, due to inconsistencies in model performance across games, this claim is unsupported by evidence.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This framework provides a collection of games that are diverse and easily adjustable. This will be referred to as the <span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">adjustments claim</span>. We show that while games are easily adjustable, there is insufficient evidence of diversity in both the original provided games and newly generated games using built-in methods.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When prompted to, language models exhibit greedy and adversarial behavior, negatively affecting group outcomes. This will be referred to as the <span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">behavioral claim</span>. We empirically verify that this claim is true through reproduction.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.SSx1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We begin by verifying these claims experimentally, followed by a discussion of their validity. We focus primarily on the <span id="S2.SSx1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">benchmark claim</span>, as this is put forward as the primary contribution of the original paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We begin by formalizing the negotiation games as described by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>, including all game variants and evaluation metrics from the original work. To reproduce the experiments within our computational constraints, we select smaller models such as GPT-4o mini and implement quantization tooling for larger open-source models. We then document critical modifications to the original open-source codebase, such as refactoring the leakage detection logic. Finally, we design experiments targeting the original claims, including extensive ablation studies, cross-game model performance comparisons, and an in-depth analysis of game adjustability.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Game Description</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As defined in the original paper, each game consists of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> distinct parties <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{p_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{p_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=6</annotation></semantics></math> by default, who negotiate over five predefined issues (e.g., building a tower). Each issue has a different number of possible sub-issue values, which represent the different possible options for an issue (e.g., making the tower 3, 4 or 5 stories tall). These issues represent various aspects of the negotiation scenario, requiring agents to deliberate and reach a consensus that satisfies their individual and collective objectives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The negotiation begins with a predefined deal from <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> (the original paper provides a default deal for each game). Afterward, players propose deals in a randomized sequence for <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> rounds (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=24</annotation></semantics></math> by default), and after the last round, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> proposes a final deal. Since the deals are proposed sequentially, we use <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote a deal proposed in the <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-th" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-th</annotation></semantics></math> round, and we denote the final deal as <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{R+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{R+1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Each agent has an associated utility function <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{p_{i}}(\cdot):\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{p_{i}}(\cdot):\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and a threshold <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{p_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{p_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>. A player can reach a maximum utility of 100 for a deal, and hence the threshold is a number between 0 and 100. A deal is said to be acceptable if its utility exceeds the threshold for at least <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N-1</annotation></semantics></math> players (5 in the case of 6 players). Furthermore, the two players with veto power, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, must also accept the deal.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Game Variants</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> we identify three primary attributes to game settings that serve to alter negotiation dynamics:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setting Updates:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A language model is prompted to generate the text for the agent prompts, which introduces the motivations of the different agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Score Function Updates:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All utility functions <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{p_{i}}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{p_{i}}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, as well as the minimum acceptable thresholds <math id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{p_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{p_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>, are manually curated by the original authors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">With these parameters, 5 pre-configured games are provided by the authors of the original paper: The <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base rewritten</span> games share the score functions but have different setting descriptions. <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Games 1</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2</span>, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3</span> have settings and score functions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agent Behavior Updates</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Another way the games change is through agent prompting. By default, agents are instructed to be cooperative and to prioritize achieving a deal. However, with the goal of evaluating the ability of models to adopt prompted behavior, agents can be prompted to assume different strategies: a greedy approach, where they prioritize maximizing their personal score, or an adversarial approach, where they actively seek to prevent a deal from being reached.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>Game Evaluation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the dynamics of the negotiation process of the agents using the same metrics as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> as well as additional metrics that we proposed, which are discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 3.2 Experiments ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>. We use the percentage of deals achieved over 20 game iterations as the primary evaluation metric. These metrics from the original paper are:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">5/6-way:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Acceptable deals proposed in the final round (i.e. whether <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(R+1)}\in\Pi_{acc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(R+1)}\in\Pi_{acc}</annotation></semantics></math>), where</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Pi_{acc}=\{\pi\in\Pi|U_{p_{1}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{1}},U_{p_{2}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{2}}\text{ and }|\{p_{i}\in P|U_{p_{i}}(\pi)&lt;\tau_{p_{i}}\}|\leq 1\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mtext> and </mtext><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">≤</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{acc}=\{\pi\in\Pi|U_{p_{1}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{1}},U_{p_{2}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{2}}\text{ and }|\{p_{i}\in P|U_{p_{i}}(\pi)&lt;\tau_{p_{i}}\}|\leq 1\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">6-way:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deals acceptable by 6 players in the final round (i.e. whether <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{(R+1)}\in\Pi_{hard}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{(R+1)}\in\Pi_{hard}</annotation></semantics></math>), given by</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Pi_{hard}=\{\pi\in\Pi|\forall p_{i}\in P,U_{p_{i}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{i}}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{hard}=\{\pi\in\Pi|\forall p_{i}\in P,U_{p_{i}}(\pi)\geq\tau_{p_{i}}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Any:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Whether at least one of the deals proposed by <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> belongs to <math id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{acc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{acc}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Leakage:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How often an agent discloses its private scoring information despite being instructed not to. In the original paper, leakage is measured using a GPT-4 model that receives the entire conversation and judges whether leakage occurred. We note that most leakage was induced by bugs, discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS5" title="3.1.5 Code Adjustments ‣ 3.1 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Wrong deals:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Proportion of deals proposed where the score of the proposing agent falls below its threshold.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.4 </span>Model Descriptions</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the original study by evaluating the benchmark on a broader range of models (including smaller and open-source architectures) to test whether the results of the benchmark remain robust beyond the originally tested systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All models are sourced from Hugging Face<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
              https://huggingface.co/</span></span></span> and used in their pre-trained form without fine-tuning. Due to computational constraints, we quantize larger models using <span id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bitsandbytes<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">2</span></span>
                  
                  
                  
                <span id="footnote2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">https://huggingface.co/docs/bitsandbytes/main/en/index</span></span></span></span></span> to fit within available resources (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, Table <a href="#A1.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ A.1 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For subsequent experiments, we filter models to only those demonstrating no leakage under the evaluation framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>. This ensures fair comparisons, as leakage corrections (discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS5" title="3.1.5 Code Adjustments ‣ 3.1 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.5</span></a>) could disproportionately affect results across models. To further assess generalizability, we also evaluate GPT-4o mini<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
              https://openai.com/index/gpt-4o-mini-advancing-cost-efficient-intelligence/</span></span></span> and GPT-4o<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
              https://openai.com/index/hello-gpt-4o/</span></span></span>, testing whether claims hold for closed-source architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.5 </span>Code Adjustments</h4>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Addressing Leakage:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original paper uses GPT-4 to process whether a score leakage has occurred in a given interaction. However, an inspection of the original implementation reveals that the reported leakage metrics are heavily confounded by structural code behavior, as opposed to purposeful goal leakage by the agents to obtain an advantage. When models deviate from formatting rules (e.g., omitting <code id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;ANSWER&gt;</code> tags), the system automatically exposes confidential outputs. This pattern was observed to comprise the bulk of reported leakage events in our runs. It remains unclear whether this is a subversive attempt by the model to gain negotiation advantage, however by separating this particular case we obtain a more interpretable and precise definition of leakage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We implement this by handling malformed public responses containing illegal keywords or missing the required structural markers. We weaken the requirements on public answer extraction, such that responses with minor formatting issues are also processed into a public answer. In the case where no valid public answer can be extracted, we terminate negotiations, exclude them from metric calculations, and log the run as a failure. This approach separately categorizes outputs containing a few commonly seen formatting errors, giving a more interpretable leakage metric. These results can be found in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Leakage Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify the remaining leakage, we flag instances where an answer contains illegal keywords such as <code id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;plan&gt;</code> or <code id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;scratchpad&gt;</code>.While the previous paragraph discusses handling malformed responses, this method explicitly focuses on measuring leakage through structured detection. In the original study, GPT-4 naturally adhered to formatting rules, avoiding leakage. However, smaller models often failed to do so, causing unintended leakage due to parsing errors. Our fix addresses this issue, enabling fair evaluation of these weaker models by ensuring their negotiation attempts are not discarded due to formatting inconsistencies. We validated our approach on GPT-4o mini, Qwen2.5-72B, and Mistral-Small, which followed the expected format and showed no leakage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While leakage remains a concern in some other architectures, our refined approach substantially mitigates its impact, ensuring that low-performing models can still be meaningfully evaluated without being unfairly penalized for formatting inconsistencies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Other Code Changes:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The criteria for deal acceptance are inconsistent. Firstly, the text specifies that a deal must “exceed” thresholds (implying strict inequality <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>), but the original implementation permits values greater than or equal to thresholds (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>), as seen in the <code id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">check_agreement</code> function. To align with their implementation, we adopt <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> in our replication. Secondly, we find that a condition within the provided evaluation script implements an unconditional relaxation of the threshold of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> by 10 units. In the prompts implemented in the original paper, it is stated that <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> can get a 10 points bonus in case of unanimity, which is not consistent with their implemented evaluation. This game variation is not introduced in the original paper aside from a mention in Appendix F, which is only meant to apply to greedy games. As this can result in inflated performance metrics by increasing the size of the feasibility set, we do not adjust the threshold of <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we identify and correct a bug in the original evaluation, where when <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> fails to propose a valid deal in the final round, the last valid deal from <math id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is by default considered as the final deal. A valid deal is thus accepted as one that can be successfully parsed, instead of a deal that while incorrectly formatted, still functions as one. This oversight leads to inflated <span id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Final</span> metrics, as non-final deals are mistakenly used in the evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">An overview of the code used to run experiments, along with a description of the changes made to improve the user experience of running multiple experiments can be found in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1.SSS1" title="A.1.1 Code Structure ‣ A.1 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Experiments</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the experiments designed to assess each claim as defined in Section <a href="#S2.SSx1" title="Claims ‣ 2 Scope of reproducibility ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Benchmark claim</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">benchmark claim</span> states that a user may use the proposed experiments as a tool to measure and compare the ability of language models to cooperate and negotiate. We assert that, for this claim to be true, these experiments must provide an interpretable comparison between models. Otherwise, it would be difficult for a user to draw conclusions about how the ability of a model to negotiate compares to another. For this purpose, the following experiments aim to both provide a more complete view of each step in the model comparison process, and of the games themselves.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Base Game Performance:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We attempt to reproduce the findings on the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base game</span>. We will refer to this experiment as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 1</span>. With this experiment, we investigate the generalizability of this benchmark to further models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablations:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the original paper, the ablation study was unclear as to the exact prompt adjustments made as well as why only a select portion of possible configurations were attempted. We reproduce the ablations performed in the original study as well as additional experiments to cover the full range of possible ablations. We will refer to this experiment as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 2</span>. We run the ablation study on more than one model, namely GPT-4o mini and Qwen2.5-72B. This is done to investigate whether an optimal ablation configuration for one model is optimal for others. As the ablated prompt templates are not provided by the authors, we create our own which can be found in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Ablation prompts ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. We detail our full ablation configurations in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extra Game Performance:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original work repeats runs for <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base, base rewritten, game 1, game 2,</span> and <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">game 3</span> to demonstrate a wider variety of performances across different games. However, there are no results for how models other than GPT4 perform on these different games.
We evaluate three models — Mistral-Small, Qwen2.5-72B, and GPT-4o mini — across all negotiation games. We selected Mistral-Small and Qwen2.5-72B in accordance with the criteria laid out in Section <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS4" title="3.1.4 Model Descriptions ‣ 3.1 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.4</span></a>, while GPT-4o mini tests generalizability to closed-source architectures. This analysis, labeled <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 3</span>, compares negotiation performance across models to assess consistency and robustness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">New evaluation metrics:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the original paper, each game reported metrics based on the number of deals accepted by five or six parties. While this approach captures broad acceptability, several frameworks exist to evaluate the success of automated negotiations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang and Ito, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Endriss et al., 2006</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanchez-Anguix et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Building on these efforts, we analyze negotiation dynamics through the lens of social welfare—a framework particularly suited to assessing fairness and efficiency in multi-agent systems. To this end, we examine three social welfare metrics: (1) Utilitarian Social Welfare (USW), which sums the utilities of all players in a deal, this metric is equivalent to the performance reported by the original paper; (2) Egalitarian Social Welfare (ESW), which considers the minimum utility among players as a measure of fairness, this targets whether the interests of a single agent are being ignored; and (3) Nash Social Welfare (NSW) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaneko and Nakamura, 1979</a>)</cite>, which multiplies individual utilities to balance efficiency and equity, observing if utility is evenly spread across agents. These metrics define the foundation of <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 4</span>, enabling a structured comparison of negotiation outcomes across different fairness paradigms. Importantly, these additional metrics are not intended as an expansion of the original benchmark; rather, they serve as a safeguard to verify that negotiations remain fair and to ensure that models do not implicitly collaborate against a single player, artificially inflating overall scores at the individual’s expense.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baseline Models:</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original work proposes a repeated rule-based baseline in which each agent, in turn, modifies a previously proposed deal by incrementally optimizing the sub-options from highest to lowest priority until its minimum threshold is reached (or no further improvements are possible). However, because the implementation for this is not available and the notion of “importance” or “priority” is insufficiently defined, producing outcomes consistent with those reported in the original paper using an intuitive notion of priority is challenging. Consequently, we introduce an easy to reproduce baseline in which issues are selected in a random sequence rather than sorted by priority, preserving all other elements of the authors’ procedure exactly as described. We refer to this as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 5</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Adjustments claim</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This claim affirms that the provided games are diverse and easily adjustable. In Section <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS2" title="3.1.2 Game Variants ‣ 3.1 Implementation Details ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.2</span></a> we categorize the three main attributes that differentiate games: setting, score function, and behavior. As the impact of behavioral differences is discussed while analyzing the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">behavioral claim</span> (Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Behavioral claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), we investigate whether the games differ greatly in the setting and score function categories and how adjustable the given games are in said categories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Regarding settings, the authors provide a prompt to generate new negotiation scenarios. After looking at the five existing games, we found that the setting in every game is based on a construction project. As there exist many other plausible negotiation settings, we investigate if alternative backgrounds are achievable with their provided prompt. To do this, we query the prompt ten times using the GPT-4 model to remain consistent with the methodology suggested by the original work. Finally, we construct an alternative version of the prompt with words such as “project” and “resources” removed to show that non-construction proposals are obtainable through the same method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As for score function updates, the original work proposes to adjust games through (1) modifying player-specific minimum thresholds, (2) changing the number of players and (3) changes in the sparsity of the score function. While the sparsity of the scoring function is noted as a potential factor, it is never clearly defined. If sparsity is interpreted as the number of 0 valued weights in the score functions, it is not easily tunable, as a change in sparsity needs to keep the same semantics inherent in the preferences of each agent. For example, the relative orderings of the scoring functions of each agent should be maintained, and trivially changing values to 0 to increase sparsity could contradict this.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Sparsity being one factor, there is no straightforward way to quantify diversity in score functions. We approach this problem in <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 6</span>, where we introduce candidate statistics:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sparsity</span>: Counts the number of zero-valued sub-options throughout all score functions, reflecting how many issues are “ignored”.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intersection over Union(IoU)</span>: Measures average pairwise overlap among agent score functions, indicating similarity in preferences. See Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F IoU Equations ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for implementation details.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Deal Space</span>: Tracks the size of the set of all acceptable deals (<math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{acc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{acc}</annotation></semantics></math>) and set of 6-way acceptable deals (<math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{hard}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{hard}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>, the authors hypothesize that differences in sparsity explain the varying model performance on different games. By defining two measures (sparsity and IoU), we investigate quantitatively if this is valid. Deal space is investigated in the original paper, and we reproduce this calculation to assist in game comparison.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The original study briefly explores varying thresholds and player count. In our work, we test these hypotheses and expand the experiment on thresholds to a wider range. We refer to these as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 7</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3 </span>Behavioral claim</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original work investigates whether agents exhibit adversarial behavior when prompted, as well as how greed affects utility distribution. Their results show that in the greedy setting, the greedy player maintains a higher utility compared to the cooperative case, while in the adversarial setting, a targeted agent experiences lower utility than when not being targeted. We quantify these effects using GPT-4o mini and Qwen2.5-72B, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, and confirm that these trends persist across models. This replication, which we term <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 8</span>, extends the generalizability of the original findings and provides a comparative evaluation of model responses to strategic behavior prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Benchmark claim</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results for <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 1</span> are detailed in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, which shows the previously defined performance metrics. The tested <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base game</span> is very close to being solved by the DeepSeek models which, even at a quantized level, achieves near 100% performance in 5- and 6-way agreement. This aligns with the <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s prediction that better performing models, improving with every new release, necessitate a benchmark capable of scaling in difficulty. 6-way agreement still remains a difficult goal to perfectly complete, but significant gains are also visible there.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, with our knowledge of the leakage bug and our subsequent fixes detailed in the methodology, we note a vastly increased variance in the <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Leaked</span> column compared to the original paper. This can be explained by the inclusion of smaller models whose responses became parse-able with our changes.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Performance of models on the <span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base game</span> measured in %. Bolded model names indicate common models, quantized, with the original study. The results of models suffixed by “*” are taken from the original study <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In other words, Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reproduces the findings of the original study using different models, showing plausible performances. Additionally we may observe that in spite of necessary quantization procedures, large models outperform their smaller, non-quantized counterparts in negotiation despite similar sizes in memory.</p>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Ablation study results. The ablation configuration used in original work for GPT-4 is highlighted in red. Large variance in performance is visible across configurations.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The results from <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 2</span> can be found in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, which demonstrates that the impact of ablation configuration varies depending on the model, highlighting the complexity of generalizing performance across different setups. Our goal with this extension is to investigate whether selecting a single ablation configuration based solely on its performance for one model might bias comparative evaluations. For instance, a configuration that leads one model to outperform another could yield opposite results when using a different configuration. Therefore, any rigorous comparison between models should explicitly account for the choice of ablation settings, as these significantly influence performance outcomes.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Performance of models across different games.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The results of <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 3</span> are in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Model performance varies inconsistently across games. For example, while Mistral-Small achieves competitive results in <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">games 1</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2</span>, its comparatively low score on <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">game 3</span> suggests task-specific limitations. Similarly, GPT-4o mini and Qwen2.5-72B struggle most with <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">game 2</span>, whereas GPT-4 and Mistral-Small find <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">game 1</span> the hardest. These disparities highlight that difficulty is linked to unseen factors in game-agent dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">From Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, it is clear that a game’s relative difficulty can vary significantly depending on the model evaluated. In other words, a game that poses challenges for one model may be easier for another, and vice versa. This variability suggests that difficulty is not consistently aligned across models. Consequently, this raises important questions regarding the validity of using one negotiation game or another as benchmarks when evaluating language models’ capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">A subset of results for <span id="S4.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 4</span> can be seen in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. To illustrate differences in score evolution, we display charts of a poor-performing and a high-performing model (in terms of game fulfillment).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#S4.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(a)</span></a> the USW for a poor-performing model is shown to decrease over time. There is a strong negative slope of -5.8 along with a high variance of 243. The combination of a steep negative gradient and high variance suggests significant instability in the negotiation process. Additionally, the low correlation coefficient indicates that while a general downward trend exists, negotiation outcomes remain inconsistent. In the case of Phi-3.5-mini, the high variability and decreasing performance over time can be attributed to conversational drift, where negotiations break down as the scope of the conversation increases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">For high-performing models, such as that shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a>, there is a lower variance, 58.2, compared to the poor-performing model, along with a positive slope of 0.877. This, combined with a relatively high correlation coefficient of 0.687, suggests more stable and linear behavior in negotiation outcomes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the results from the ESW and Nash Equilibrium metrics largely mimic the pattern of the USW metric, verifying that one model is not exclusively dominating the rounds.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:211.4pt;">
<p id="S4.SS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The results for <span id="S4.SS1.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 5</span> are displayed in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. We compare the performance of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s baseline and our newly introduced baseline across all game variants. Our attempts to replicate their baseline did not yield results matching those reported in the original study. However, we provide an alternative, equally interpretable method demonstrating performance levels comparable to the original baseline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:211.4pt;">

<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Baseline proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> and our baseline evaluated on different game variants.</figcaption>
</figure>
      
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Although our primary goal was to replicate the original baseline, our difficulty in doing so and the lack of a clear definition of importance prompted us to propose a new, fully reproducible baseline. This does not negate the value of the original method; rather, it underscores that multiple algorithmic baselines are feasible. Based on the results, which are comparable to those reported for the original paper, and the fact that our method offers both accessibility and reproducibility, our proposed method can serve as an effective, interpretable alternative.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p14.1" class="ltx_p">In the context of this benchmark, which seeks to assess negotiation abilities, defining an appropriate baseline is nontrivial. Since a rule-based algorithm capable of solving the game can be readily implemented, the key challenge is not merely evaluating a model’s mathematical ability to negotiate but capturing the subtleties of human negotiation, such as deception, bargaining, and strategic withholding of information. A rule-based approach serves as a plausible example of rational behavior in negotiation but may fail to reflect the nuanced decision-making observed in human interactions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Adjustments claim</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Regarding prompting the model to change settings, we find that the construction project setting appears not only in the five original games but also in all ten additional games generated using the prompt from the original work. This consistency suggests an inherent bias in the prompt, which always steers the negotiation scenario toward a construction project. By removing specific terms such as “project” and “resources”, we observe a broader range of negotiation contexts emerging, revealing the extent of this bias. With our revised prompt (see Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Alternative Prompt ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>), we identify a more diverse set of negotiation settings, including e.g. discussions on military spending budgets for the upcoming year and planning a conference, where aspects like floor allocation and catering must be negotiated. The results clearly demonstrate that the negotiation scenarios generated with the original prompt are not diverse, and that adjustments are needed to obtain true diversity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As for score function updates, Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.2 Adjustments claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the results of <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 6</span>, which examines the diversity of the provided games. From a structural standpoint, these metrics reveal that, although each configuration exhibits slight numerical differences, they fall within a fairly narrow range overall. We note that the fraction of acceptable deals <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left|\Pi_{\text{acc}}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mtext>acc</mtext></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\Pi_{\text{acc}}\right|</annotation></semantics></math> is almost identical for all games by design <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which does not contribute to the claim that the games are diverse. Similarly, the fraction of hard-acceptable deals <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left|\Pi_{\text{hard}}\right|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mtext>hard</mtext></msub><mo>|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left|\Pi_{\text{hard}}\right|</annotation></semantics></math> remains relatively small across all cases. Sparsity shows moderate fluctuation, while the intersection-over-union measure ranges from about 18.75% to 29.77%, suggesting that, while differences exist in preference overlap and zero-valued options, they are not substantial. These results indicate that each setup retains comparable intrinsic characteristics.</p>
</div>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Score function statistics.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The fact that the computed statistics do not span the entire range of possible values (e.g., 0 to 100 for percentage-based metrics) is not, by itself, sufficient to conclude that they lack diversity. To establish that the games are diverse in terms of these statistics, a larger set of games should be generated, including cases where some statistics cover a wider section of possible values. These new games should be tested to determine whether they reach a saturation point in performance, either becoming trivially easy or outright impossible. If this occurs, it would indicate that including games with such statistics is redundant and that the full spectrum of meaningful values has been effectively covered.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The results for <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 7</span> are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Adjustments claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, where we examine how easily adjustable games are using the modifiers provided by original authors. The results are consistent with the findings of the original paper: in Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf1" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Adjustments claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a> performance tends to increase consistently with a decrease in the minimum threshold per player. Similarly, we find that more agreements are reached with a lower number of players, see Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf2" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Adjustments claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F2.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18230v1/media/varying_thresholds.png" id="S4.F2.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:260/155;" width="260" height="155" alt="Refer to caption">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F2.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18230v1/media/varying_players.png" id="S4.F2.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:260/155;" width="260" height="155" alt="Refer to caption">
