</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Varying thresholds and number of players in <span id="S4.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">base game</span> for GPT-4o mini</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Behavioral claim</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the results of <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 8</span>, reproducing the adversarial behavioral experiments. Consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we observe that performance declines when all players are greedy, presumably because mutual self-interest stalls compromise. Similarly, when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is greedy, we also see diminished performance, because <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> wields veto power and makes the final proposal—thus it can block suboptimal agreements until it secures a favorable share.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We note a surprising result, where we find that when a particular player—namely the Environmental League—is greedy, GPT-4o mini and Qwen2.5-72B show an increase in 5/6-way deals. One possible explanation is that these models, when facing a single (but not first-mover) greedy party, adjust their negotiation strategy in ways that induce earlier concessions or more expansive coalitions among the other players—ultimately raising the rate of larger multi-party agreements despite the Environmental League’s hardened stance.</p>
</div>

</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Evolution of deals for several behavioral configurations. <span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environmental League</span> is <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and acts as greedy for the greedy experiment and as adversarial in both the untargeted and targeted experiments. For the latter, <span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Local Labour Union</span> is the target.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also reproduce trends in game evolution with respect to the players of interest (i.e., the greedy, adversarial, and targeted players) in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Behavioral claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. For the cooperative case, we observe that <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environmental League</span> is more willing to compromise, as indicated by its lower utility. Conversely, when prompted to adopt a greedy strategy, the affected agent maintains a higher individual score. In the adversarial experiments, the utility for <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Local Labour Union</span> is lower in the targeted case, demonstrating the impact of adversarial play.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These trends become apparent when comparing model performance. In the <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> greedy setting, the last round’s distance between the greedy agent and the aggregated USW was 12.86 for GPT-4o mini but significantly higher (24.85) for Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, indicating that Qwen enforces greedy behavior more strongly. Similarly, in the untargeted adversarial setting, the distance between the would-be targeted agent and aggregated USW was -33.91 for GPT-4o mini, whereas for Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, it was only -14.03. These results indicate that stronger models like Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct better capture prompt-induced behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The benchmarking framework proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> comprises a complex simulation environment that evaluates LLM negotiation. By choosing a more complicated environment model based on a negotiation game used to teach humans, they overcome a problem inherent in related works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Akata et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brookins and DeBacker, 2023</a>)</cite>: that the simulated games are not complex enough to
represent reality. Furthermore, utilizing LLMs in a negotiation setting designed for humans opens the door to analyzing human-LLM interaction through the lens of behavioral game theory. Additionally, the extensibility of the framework helps to maintain its relevance in this era of increasingly powerful LLMs. However, this approach also comes at a cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One key challenge is that, due to its complexity and extensibility, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduces a potentially infinite number of comparison axes through their various games, which makes comparative performance across multiple games difficult to interpret, as demonstrated in our experiments, particularly in <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 3</span>. Additionally, it complicates the application of established formalisms, such as Nash Equilibrium analysis, which is commonly used in other benchmark studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brookins and DeBacker, 2023</a>)</cite>. The absence of such formal criteria further hinders the objective assessment of benchmark results. In our evaluation of the <span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmark Claim</span> and <span id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adjustments Claim</span>, we have demonstrated various practical examples of this difficulty in interpreting benchmark results. This includes factors such as our ablation analysis in <span id="S5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 2</span>, and the demonstrated weaknesses in diversity of the provided games in <span id="S5.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 6</span>. Through our extensions, we have provided additional context to the benchmark such as transparency on the previously mentioned factors as well as metrics from social welfare to assist a user in further understanding the benchmark results. Additionally, while the various minor bugs in the original implementations do not invalidate the results of the original paper, they potentially pose problems to users evaluating weaker models. By fixing them, we increase the potential audienceof this benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One potential idea for future work is developing metrics capable of describing and categorizing the various components of different negotiation games. A particularly useful example within the current framework would be a categorization of games that aligns with model performance. This would allow model developers to claim, for instance, that their new LLM outperforms others in specific game categories but not in others. Another exciting avenue of future work is to explore benchmarking the adversarial behavior of the agents through the framework by creating a “robustness against adversarial attack” metric, in order to quantitatively compare the resilience in the adversarial setting introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi et al. (2024)</a></cite>. An example of a potential metric could be the percentage of 5-way successful games, weighted by sparsity, in an adversarial environment with a single agent causing issues. We leave these potential works as ideas for further increasing the utility of this benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Appendix</h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Model Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe the models used in our experiments in Table <a href="#A1.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ A.1 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Some models were distilled from a larger model, as shown in column 3, and some models were also quantized for quicker run time considering computation constraints. The level of quantization was primarily determined by computational and memory constraints; whenever feasible, a less aggressive quantization (i.e. int8) was employed, though larger models necessitated int4 quantization. Details can be found in Table <a href="#A1.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ A.1 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.1 </span>Code Structure</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both the original and our codebase are structured into multiple Python scripts, each handling a specific aspect of the experimental process. The main script, main.py, serves as the entry point, integrating all components to execute experiments. Supporting modules manage agent behavior, negotiation rounds, prompt generation, and data handling. Detailed documentation of the code structure is available in the README file of the GitHub repository.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Initially, configuration options were managed through a combination of command-line arguments and external configuration files. The command-line arguments allow users to specify parameters such as temperature, number of agents, number of issues, number of rounds, game name, and model name. Additionally, each game directory contains a <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">config.txt</span> file that defines the setup for each agent, including their name, associated files, role, incentive, and model. This structure enables customization of experiments by modifying both command-line inputs and configuration files.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, to further enhance configurability and streamline the experimental workflow, several improvements have been introduced beyond this initial approach. Previously, the specification of models and incentives for agents was handled by modifying the game’s configuration file. However, due to the frequent need to rerun the same game with different model and incentive configurations, the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–model</span> and <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–incentive</span> command-line parameters have been added to simplify the process and reduce manual intervention. Additionally, the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–quantization</span> parameter has been introduced to enable quantization for Hugging Face models, improving performance and reducing memory requirements. To address concerns regarding sensitive information disclosure during negotiations, the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–restrict_leakage</span> flag has been implemented, with further details provided in the respective section of the report. A <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–dry_run</span> option has also been included to facilitate testing and debugging by disabling actual API calls to language models, allowing users to inspect prompts without incurring computational costs. Furthermore, environmental sustainability considerations have been incorporated into the framework through the integration of the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">codecarbon</span> EmissionsTracker, which records the carbon footprint of experiments, with the option to specify project names via the <span id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">–emission_project</span> parameter. These enhancements build upon the initial configuration system, providing a more efficient, scalable, and environmentally conscious framework for conducting negotiation experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Computational Details</h3>

<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hardware Setup</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments were conducted using local machines equipped with NVIDIA A100 and A6000 GPUs, with memory capacities of 40 GB and 48 GB, respectively. The computational resources were sufficient to accommodate all models tested, with the most demanding model requiring a maximum of 48 GB of VRAM. Thus, the experiments can be reproduced on a system with similar GPU specifications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Runtime Measurements</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The runtime for each negotiation session varied depending on the model used. Table <a href="#A1.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Runtime Measurements ‣ A.2 Computational Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation details ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents the average runtime per model for a complete negotiation session comprising 24 rounds. It was observed that computational resource demands varied significantly among different models, with some lightweight models requiring considerably fewer resources compared to larger models.</p>
</div>

<td id="A1.T9.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding:-0.45pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T9.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Llama-2-13b-chat-h</span></td>
<td id="A1.T9.2.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:-0.45pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T9.2.9.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">11</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T9.2.10" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A1.T9.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:-0.45pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T9.2.10.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">8</span></td></tr>

<td id="A1.T9.2.14.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:-0.45pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A1.T9.2.14.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">65</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Average runtime per negotiation session (24 rounds) across different models.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The total time required to complete all experimental runs, including different game variants, amounted to 422 hours. For open-source models, the total GPU/CPU hours required were 386 hours. For GPT-4o mini, the OpenAI API was utilized, resulting in different resource consumption patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Storage Requirements</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The primary storage requirement for the experiments was to store the downloaded pretrained model weights. By storing one model at a time, the total storage demand was limited to approximately 300 GB. All experiment outputs and logs were stored for post-hoc evaluation and further analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Software Environment</h5>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments were conducted on Linux-based systems. For OpenAI models (i.e., GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini), the OpenAI API was utilized, whereas for open-source models, the Hugging Face <span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transformers</span> library was employed. Additionally, the <span id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">codecarbon</span> library was used to monitor carbon emissions during the computational processes.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Ablation prompts</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present here the prompts used to create the Chain of Thought for the agents. These variations were used to recreate and extend the ablation study, see Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Benchmark claim ‣ 4 Results ‣ [Re] Benchmarking LLM Capabilities in Negotiation through Scoreable Games" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Previous Deals</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt to consider previous deals is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Please use the scratchpad for the following: Given the history of previous suggested deals, calculate your scores for each past suggested deal in the history.
Then, use these deals to further reason about your next proposed deal.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Others Preferences</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt to consider the preferences of other players is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">In your scratchpad,
1) think about what others may prefer,
2) Based on others’ preferences and history and your notes, propose one proposal that balances between your scores and accommodating others and that is more likely to lead to an agreement.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Candidates</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt to generate three deal candidates before choosing one is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Please use the scratchpad for the following: Before suggesting a final deal, display three possible deals to suggest while keeping in mind your objectives, and number them with (1), (2), and (3).
When your final deal is made, choose one of these three deals.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Planning</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt to release a plan at each round is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">After the final answer, building on your current move and analysis,
briefly write down short notes for yourself of what exact options you can explore the next time you speak.
Enclose the notes between &lt;PLAN&gt; and &lt;/PLAN&gt;.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Carbon Emissions</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Environmental sustainability considerations have been incorporated into our framework through the integration of the <span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">codecarbon<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">5</span></span>
              
              
              
            <span id="footnote5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif">https://codecarbon.io/</span></span></span></span></span> emissions tracker, which records the carbon footprint of experiments by considering the specifications of the system running the model, the carbon efficiency of the country it is powered in, and electricity usage. By extrapolating the results of running the carbon tracker for each model on a set of 20 games, the total cost of our runs are approximately <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="48.7kg\text{ }CO_{2}e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>48.7</mn><mi>k</mi><mi>g</mi><mtext> </mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>O</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">48.7kg\text{ }CO_{2}e</annotation></semantics></math>. We used 24 million input and 28 million output tokens of GPT-4o mini.
We now state the carbon emissions that our experiments entailed.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T10" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Carbon</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{2})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=2.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>2.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=2.0</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A3.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{6})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Carbon</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{6})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=8.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>8.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=8.0</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A3.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{10})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Carbon</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{Carbon}(T_{10})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A3.Ex7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=7.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>7.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=7.8</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">And thus the final calculated carbon output is</p>
<table id="A3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\text{Total Carbon Emissions}=48.7kg\text{ }CO_{2}e" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Total Carbon Emissions</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>48.7</mn><mi>k</mi><mi>g</mi><mtext> </mtext><mi>C</mi><mi>O</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Total Carbon Emissions}=48.7kg\text{ }CO_{2}e</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">These emissions are approximately equivalent to those produced by driving a Ford F-150 for 117 miles, which is roughly the distance between Rotterdam and Groningen.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We also used GPT-4o mini. However as the running cost for running this model is unknown, we exclude it from the calculation.</p>
</div>

</section>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After applying our method to the original experiments and manually verifying outcomes, we find that our strategy significantly reduces leakage, lowering the associated metrics by up to 69.42% compared to the original approach. Furthermore, our refined method results in lower 5/6-way agreement rates, as agents no longer have unintended access to private information that could facilitate deal-making. While no detection framework is entirely exhaustive, our improvements offer a substantial reduction in risk of leakage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Social Welfare Definitions</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a score function such that each deal is assigned a natural number value under some utility <math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}(\pi):\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}(\pi):\Pi\rightarrow\mathbb{N}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<ol id="A5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Utilitarian Social Welfare (USW):</span> Aggregates each player’s utility for a deal, as in the original study, but does not consider fairness.</p>
<table id="A5.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\mathrm{usw}}(\pi)=\sum_{p_{i}\in P}U_{p_{i}}(\pi)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>usw</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\mathrm{usw}}(\pi)=\sum_{p_{i}\in P}U_{p_{i}}(\pi)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Egalitarian Social Welfare (ESW):</span> Ensures all players benefit by taking the minimum utility across players for each deal.</p>
<table id="A5.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\mathrm{esw}}(\pi)=\min_{p_{i}\in P}\bigl\{\,U_{p_{i}}(\pi)\bigr\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>esw</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\mathrm{esw}}(\pi)=\min_{p_{i}\in P}\bigl\{\,U_{p_{i}}(\pi)\bigr\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="A5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Nash Social Welfare (NSW):</span> Promotes fairness by multiplying players’ utilities, favoring even distributions (e.g., <math id="A5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4&gt;2\times 6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4&gt;2\times 6</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
<table id="A5.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\mathrm{nsw}}(\pi)=\prod_{p_{i}\in P}U_{p_{i}}(\pi)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>nsw</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\mathrm{nsw}}(\pi)=\prod_{p_{i}\in P}U_{p_{i}}(\pi)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ol>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>IoU Equations</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Intersection over Union (IoU) metric quantifies similarity between agent scoring functions by measuring the overlap in their preferences. Pairwise IoU computes the ratio of shared valuations between two agents, while the overall IoU aggregates these values across all agent pairs. The following equations formally define these computations, as referenced in <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experiment 6</span>, to assess preference alignment and diversity.</p>
<table id="A6.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{IoU}=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p_{x}\in P}\frac{1}{|P\textbackslash\{p_{x}\}|}\sum_{p_{y}\in P\textbackslash\{p_{x}\}}\text{Pairwise IoU}(p_{x},p_{y})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>IoU</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>\</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>\</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mrow><mtext>Pairwise IoU</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{IoU}=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p_{x}\in P}\frac{1}{|P\textbackslash\{p_{x}\}|}\sum_{p_{y}\in P\textbackslash\{p_{x}\}}\text{Pairwise IoU}(p_{x},p_{y})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="A6.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pairwise IoU}(p_{x},p_{y})=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i=1}^{|I|}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{|I_{j}|}\min(p_{x,i_{j}},p_{y,i_{j}})}{\sum_{k=1}^{|I_{k}|}\max(p_{x,i_{k}},p_{y,i_{k}})}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Pairwise IoU</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pairwise IoU}(p_{x},p_{y})=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i=1}^{|I|}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{|I_{j}|}\min(p_{x,i_{j}},p_{y,i_{j}})}{\sum_{k=1}^{|I_{k}|}\max(p_{x,i_{k}},p_{y,i_{k}})}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Alternative Prompt</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">You are an expert in negotiation games and have read many books on the subject. Please help me in creating a negotiation game. The game consists of 6 players (party 1, party 2, party 3, etc.) who are negotiating over 5 issues. Each of the 5 issues has different sub-options (2 issues have 3 options, 2 issues have 4 options, 1 issue has 5 options). One of the players makes a first proposal. The issues involve the impact of the negotiated outcome on stakeholders. The other players represent different parties with competing interests. The parties must not include a mediator. The issues represent the interests of other parties. The issues do not necessarily have a one-to-one mapping to each party; different parties might have similar or competing interests under each issue (e.g., one wants more funding, one wants less funding, etc.). Some parties do not care at all about certain issues (they only care about a subset of issues). The game is based on cooperative bargaining. Your task is to create the background story and the role of each party according to the previously mentioned guidelines. Please indicate their general goals and motivations and their objectives from the negotiation. You should also create the issues they are negotiating over (please name them issues A, B, etc.) by specifying the different sub-options (A1, B1, C1, etc.). For each issue, please specify what the preferences of each of the parties are over the issues and why they prefer so (e.g., Party 1 prefers A3 then A2 then A4, etc.). Please also assign priorities of the issues to each party and explain why (e.g., Party 1 cares the most about issue A, they do not care about issue D). Please also indicate if an issue is much more important than the others. Make it interesting with lots of potential for cooperation and competition between parties!! Make the issues and options have some implications over generally more than one party involved, but you can have some parties with no interest at all in some issues. Remember that it is a cooperative non-zero-sum game.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
